# High Idle While Coasting in Neutral

A high idle that manifests only while coasting in neutral or clutch disengaged, but resolves once the vehicle is stationary, points to a specific hydraulic or vacuum imbalance rather than a generic engine management failure. In your 1999 Chevrolet Camaro with the 5.7-liter V8, the symptom of dropping from 1400â1800 RPM only after coming to a complete stop suggests the idle air control (IAC) system is compensating for an unintended load or vacuum leak that vanishes when the engine reaches zero speed.

When you are coasting, the engine must maintain enough torque to overcome internal friction and air resistance. If there is a vacuum leak on the intake manifold gasket or PCV valve, the Engine Control Module (ECM) detects a lean condition and opens the IAC valve wider to increase airflow and raise RPMs to compensate. Once you stop and apply the brakes, the engine load drops to zero, and if the leak isn't severe enough to trigger a persistent fault code while idling, the ECM might retract the IAC slightly, but often the residual vacuum or pressure dynamics keep it elevated until the thermal or hydraulic state stabilizes at a complete halt.

The fact that you disconnected the battery and the Check Engine Light cleared indicates that no current fault codes are being stored. This is a critical diagnostic clue: if the high idle were caused by a massive vacuum leak, the ECM would likely have logged a fuel trim code (P0171 or P0174) immediately upon reconnection. The absence of these codes suggests the issue is either intermittent, temperature-dependent, or related to the Idle Air Control valve itself sticking in an open position due to carbon buildup or electrical drift.

### Inspecting the IAC Valve and Plenum

The most direct approach is to inspect the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve on the throttle body. On GM 5.7-liter engines of this era, the IAC is a stepper motor that controls bypass air around the throttle plate. Over time, carbon deposits can coat the pintle inside the valve, causing it to stick or fail to return to its closed position properly when commanded by the ECM.

To test this without removing the part, you can disconnect the electrical connector from the IAC valve and ground it temporarily while the engine is running and in neutral. If the RPM drops significantly and stabilizes near 800â900 RPM, the IAC pintle is likely stuck open or failing to close. If the RPM spikes even higher when grounded, the IAC motor itself may be faulty and trying to drive against the ground signal.

Alternatively, you can clean the throttle body and IAC valve with a dedicated carburetor cleaner. This is often effective for engines that have accumulated significant deposits from burning oil or long-term idling. After cleaning, reassemble carefully and ensure the gasket is seated correctly to avoid creating a new vacuum leak.

### Checking Vacuum Lines and PCV System

If cleaning the IAC does not resolve the issue, inspect all vacuum lines connected to the intake manifold and brake booster. A cracked hose can introduce enough air to raise the idle while coasting but might not be large enough to trigger a fault code immediately. Pay special attention to the PCV valve; if it is stuck open, it creates a significant load on the engine during deceleration or coasting.

Another possibility specific to your scenario is the transmission torque converter lock-up solenoid. If the converter is slipping slightly in neutral due to a failing solenoid or internal clutch pack issues, it can create a parasitic load that forces the ECM to raise idle speed to prevent stalling. However, since this happens only in neutral and not while driving (where the transmission is locked), this is less likely unless the issue is isolated to the neutral circuit.

### Electrical Grounding Issues

Do not overlook grounding points. A poor ground on the IAC valve harness or the ECU can cause erratic voltage readings, leading the ECM to misinterpret the valve's position and command a higher duty cycle. Check the grounds near the throttle body and under the engine bay for corrosion or loose connections.

If the problem persists after these mechanical checks, consider using an OBD-II scanner with live data capabilities. Monitor the Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) and Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT). If you see a positive fuel trim (e.g., +10% to +15%) while coasting in neutral but near 0% when stopped, it confirms the ECM is actively enriching the mixture to compensate for an air leak or high load. This data will pinpoint whether the root cause is an intake leak or a component failure requiring replacement.

Addressing this issue early prevents potential stalling at low speeds and ensures the engine management system remains within its designed operational parameters.
